My research focuses on labor markets, poverty, education, and the use of new
data sources for economic measurement.

::: {.research-item}
## Job Quality and Poverty in Developing Countries: Evidence from Côte d’Ivoire

**Working paper** · [Read the paper](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jo8JqBBzvfliCmEQC0UG4NHShR-NiNCe/view?usp=sharing)

Using the 2018 Harmonized Survey of Household Living Conditions, this study
examines how the quality of jobs held by household members relates to household
poverty. The results suggest that better employment conditions—particularly
women’s access to high-quality jobs—can reduce poverty risk.
:::

::: {.research-item}
## The Causal Impact of Armed Conflict on Education Outcomes in Mali

*With Josias Sadia*

**Working paper** · [Read the paper](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1kvELyRo6ru2XATIfZkzbS5NQ27Km8HPY/view?usp=sharing)

Using difference-in-differences and propensity score matching, this study
analyzes the effects of Mali’s prolonged crises on educational attainment. It
finds a decline of 1.13 to 1.97 years of education among generations who were of
school age during the conflict.
:::

::: {.research-item}
## Exposure to Violence and Academic Performance Among Adolescents in Côte d’Ivoire

*With Sekongo Coulibaly*

**Working paper** · [Read the paper](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1hsOuKR41ZenMkJwZHB-_QiBoDGeIZ5N1/view?usp=sharing)

Using the 2018 Violence Against Children Survey, this paper studies academic
outcomes among children aged 13 to 18. Exposure to violence is associated with
greater risks of grade repetition and school dropout, underlining the need to
connect education policy with child-protection measures.
:::

::: {.research-item}
## Estimating Poverty with Satellite Imagery in Developing Countries: Evidence from Côte d’Ivoire

*With Kone Kinin Mamadou*

**Working paper** · [Read the paper](https://gouvci-my.sharepoint.com/:b:/g/personal/j_migone_stat_plan_gouv_ci/IQCuKg5LwElMSKoG3dK40V69AcFoFGnZSRnBp4MiBgEz0wk?e=tdONmd)

This study combines Sentinel-2 imagery, transfer learning, and household survey
data to estimate poverty between survey waves. The preferred model closely
reproduces the observed national poverty rates for 2018 and 2021, illustrating
how satellite data can complement traditional welfare monitoring.
:::
